subject: Coffee & Tea
title: All Tea Comes From One Plant
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: All Tea Comes From One Plant.

hook.text: Green, black, white, oolong, pu-erh—every true tea comes from a single species: Camellia sinensis.

buildup.text: The difference between types isn't the plant. It's how the leaves are processed after picking.

discovery.text: Oxidation is the key. Stopping it early gives green tea. Letting it run fully gives black tea.

twist.text: Herbal 'teas' like chamomile and rooibos aren't tea at all. They're infusions from other plants, called tisanes.

climax.text: One plant, processed six different ways, produces the entire spectrum of tea flavors.

punchline.text: One leaf, infinite possibilities. Processing is everything.

quiz.question: What determines the type of tea (green, black, etc.)?
options: How the leaves are processed, especially oxidation

details.summary: Every type of true tea, whether black, green, white, oolong, or pu-erh, comes from the same species: Camellia sinensis. The enormous diversity of flavor, color, and aroma arises not from different plants but from how and where the leaves are grown, harvested, and processed.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing that one plant produces all tea transforms how you understand the drink. Processing, not botany, creates the variety on your shelf.
takeaways: All true tea comes from Camellia sinensis
Processing determines whether leaves become black, green, or white tea
Herbal infusions like chamomile are technically not tea

faq.question: What is the difference between tea and herbal tea?
faq.answer: True tea comes from Camellia sinensis leaves. Herbal teas, or tisanes, are infusions of other plants like chamomile, rooibos, or peppermint. They contain no actual tea leaves and are caffeine-free unless the herb itself contains caffeine.

faq.question: How many varieties of tea exist worldwide?
faq.answer: Thousands of distinct teas exist, differentiated by cultivar, growing region, harvest timing, and processing technique. China alone produces hundreds of named varieties. The six main categories are green, black, white, oolong, yellow, and dark (pu-erh) tea.
